g: Russian novel; comic and melancholy character study
sum: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, a kind-hearted, dreamy landowner in St Petersburg, cannot bring himself to get out of bed, let alone manage his estate or answer his letters. His energetic friend Stolz and the lively Olga try to rouse him into love and action, but Oblomov keeps drifting back toward sleep, comfort and memories of a childhood idyll.
bg: Ivan Goncharov published the novel in 1859, after years of work. It was an immediate sensation, and the word oblomovshchina, Oblomovism, entered Russian as a term for apathetic inertia, especially among the gentry. Goncharov also worked for decades as a government censor.
br: The first part, in which Oblomov barely leaves his sofa, is famously long and comic; persevere, because the novel deepens and saddens as it goes on. The chapter called Oblomov’s Dream is a highlight.
la: Goncharov combines gentle comedy with real tenderness, so Oblomov is both ridiculous and lovable, and the contrast with the hardworking Stolz is never simply a moral lesson. Long descriptive passages slow time down deliberately.
cx: Written just before the emancipation of the serfs in 1861, the novel was read as a diagnosis of a landowning class living off unfree labour and unable to act.
th: Inertia and fear
Oblomov’s idleness hides fear of a demanding, disappointing world.
Love and change
Olga tries to awaken him, and both are changed by the attempt.
Nostalgia
Childhood comfort can become a lifelong refuge and trap.
fit: A quieter, funnier Russian classic that balances the intensity of Dostoevsky on your list.
mis: Slow by design, especially the opening, and readers who want plot may lose patience.
rq: What does Olga see in him?
Is Stolz meant to be admired?
dq: Is Oblomov a failure or a kind of sage?
Do you recognise Oblomovism in modern life?
rel: Turgenev’s Fathers and Sons, another portrait of generations.

sum: In the One State, a glass city sealed off from nature, citizens live by a Table of Hours, have numbers instead of names, and are allowed love only by coupon. The engineer D-503, building a spaceship to carry the State’s reason to other worlds, records his thoughts in a journal, until the mysterious I-330 awakens in him an imagination and desire his world has outlawed.
bg: Yevgeny Zamyatin wrote We around 1920–21 in Soviet Russia. It was banned there and first published in English translation in New York in 1924; it did not appear in Russia until 1988. It directly influenced Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four and resembles Huxley’s Brave New World.
br: The journal format and D-503’s mathematical language take some adjustment. Read it as a record of a mind slowly cracking open; the strangeness of the style is part of the point.
la: Zamyatin writes in fragmented, elliptical prose full of mathematical imagery and colour symbolism, so that the narrator’s emotional awakening is felt in the breakdown of his rational language.
cx: The novel satirised the early Soviet ideal of rational, collective, industrialised life, and Zamyatin, an engineer and former Bolshevik, was eventually forced into exile in 1931.
th: Freedom and happiness
The State claims that freedom and happiness are incompatible.
Reason and imagination
Imagination is treated as a disease to be cured.
The individual and the collective
D-503 discovers a self the State tried to erase.
fit: The founding dystopia, a fascinating link between the Russian classics and the science fiction on your list.
mis: Its fragmented style can be hard going, and readers who know Orwell may find some ideas familiar.
rq: What does the Green Wall represent?
dq: Is the One State’s bargain ever tempting?
How does We compare with Nineteen Eighty-Four?

sum: Lyubov Ranevskaya returns from Paris to her family’s heavily mortgaged estate, famous for its cherry orchard, just before it is to be auctioned. The merchant Lopakhin, whose father was a serf on the estate, urges her to save it by cutting down the orchard for summer cottages, but the family cannot bring themselves to act as the auction day approaches.
bg: Anton Chekhov’s final play premiered at the Moscow Art Theatre in January 1904, months before his death from tuberculosis. Chekhov called it a comedy and argued with director Stanislavski, who staged it as tragedy. It has been staged continuously ever since.
br: Read it aloud or imagine it staged; much of its meaning lies in pauses, offhand remarks and what characters avoid saying. A good recent translation reads naturally as speech.
la: Chekhov builds drama from indirect dialogue, characters talking past one another, and the famous offstage sound of a breaking string, letting comedy and sorrow coexist. Characters are often comic in their self-absorption, yet each is given a moment of genuine feeling.
cx: The play captures the decline of the Russian landed gentry after the emancipation of the serfs and the rise of a new merchant class, on the eve of the 1905 revolution.
th: Change and loss
An old way of life ends whether or not anyone acts.
Memory and denial
The family clings to the orchard as a symbol of the past.
Class and history
A former serf’s son becomes master of the estate.
fit: A short, rich play that pairs with Chekhov’s stories already on your list.
mis: Plays can be hard to imagine on the page, and its lack of conventional action puzzles some readers.
rq: Why can’t Ranevskaya save the orchard?
Is Lopakhin a villain or a hero?
What does the breaking string mean?
dq: Is the play a comedy or a tragedy?
What does the orchard symbolise for each character?

g: Russian play; drama of provincial life
sum: On a remote country estate, Vanya and his niece Sonya have worked for years to send money to the retired professor Serebryakov, Vanya’s former brother-in-law, whom they once revered. When the professor arrives with his beautiful young wife Yelena, Vanya realises he has wasted his life on a fraud, and desire, resentment and despair surface among everyone in the house.
bg: Anton Chekhov reworked an earlier play, The Wood Demon, into Uncle Vanya, published in 1897 and staged by the Moscow Art Theatre in 1899. It has become one of the most performed plays in the world. Louis Malle’s film Vanya on 42nd Street is a celebrated adaptation.
br: Short enough to read in one sitting. Notice the conversations about forests, work and the future, especially from the doctor Astrov, and save time for Sonya’s famous closing speech.
la: Chekhov uses everyday conversation, missed connections and long pauses to reveal inner lives; the drama lies in emotions barely acknowledged rather than in events. Tension rises toward one explosive scene, then subsides into routine.
cx: The play reflects provincial Russian gentry life, Chekhov’s own experience as a country doctor, and early concern with deforestation, voiced by Astrov. Astrov’s ecological speeches feel strikingly modern.
th: Wasted lives
Vanya realises too late that he has served a false idol.
Work and endurance
Sonya finds meaning in patient labour and faith.
Desire and loneliness
Everyone longs for someone who cannot return it.
fit: A companion to The Cherry Orchard and The Seagull, rounding out your Chekhov.
mis: Its quietness and lack of plot may feel uneventful to readers who prefer drama on the page.
cw: A gun is fired in anger.
rq: Why does Astrov care so much about forests?
What does Sonya’s final speech offer?
dq: Is the play hopeful or despairing?
Who is the most sympathetic character, and why?

g: Russian play; drama of art and love
sum: At a lakeside estate, the young writer Konstantin stages an experimental play starring Nina, the girl he loves, hoping to impress his mother, the famous actress Arkadina, and her lover, the successful novelist Trigorin. The performance fails, and over the following years love, ambition and art entangle all four in disappointments symbolised by a shot seagull.
bg: Anton Chekhov’s play failed disastrously at its 1896 premiere in St Petersburg, but triumphed in 1898 at the newly founded Moscow Art Theatre, which adopted the seagull as its emblem. It was the first of his four major plays.
br: Short enough for one sitting. Watch the arguments about art, old and new forms, fame and vocation, and notice how much happens offstage, between acts. The final act is set two years after the third.
la: Chekhov mixes comedy and tragedy, ironic dialogue and symbolism, and lets major events happen out of sight, so the audience sees mostly the aftermath. Quoted lines from Hamlet underline the theme of art and family conflict.
cx: The play reflects debates about new forms in theatre and literature at the end of the nineteenth century, and Chekhov’s own experiences of literary life and failure.
th: Art and ambition
Characters argue over what art is for and what it costs.
Love unreturned
Almost everyone loves someone who loves someone else.
Endurance
Nina learns that what matters is the ability to endure.
fit: Completes your Chekhov trio and pairs with the writing-craft books for its debates about art.
mis: Its offstage action and shifting tone may feel elusive on the page. Characters can seem self-absorbed.
rq: How do Konstantin and Trigorin differ as writers?
How has Nina changed by the end?
dq: Is the play a comedy, as Chekhov called it?
What does it say about art and fame?
